Never allow caching to cross user or data boundaries in a way that exposes private content.

sections.title: Where it fits
paragraphs: Track request volume, input and output use, cache use, retrieval work, and retries. Set budgets or quotas at the right application boundary. Reduce unnecessary context before reducing answer quality. Route simple tasks to an adequate lower-cost model only after evaluation.

sections.title: Failure and control
paragraphs: Use cost per successful task as a decision measure. This includes retries, review, and correction. Compare designs with the same task set and quality threshold.

sections.title: Causal worked trace
paragraphs: Causal trace: A request repeats a stable prompt prefix and adds a changing user question. A supported model path can reuse eligible prefix computation through prompt caching. The service reports cache-related usage where supported. The application pays for remaining input, output, retrieval, and orchestration work. If the changing content appears before the stable prefix, cache reuse can decline.

sections.title: Failure diagnosis
paragraphs: Failure diagnosis: Check model support, API configuration, cache eligibility, prefix order, and returned usage signals. Compare a repeated stable prefix with a changed prefix. If cost remains high, inspect total request volume, output length, retrieval, retries, and agent calls. Do not assume caching removes the cost of all work.

sections.title: Transfer case and misconception
paragraphs: Transfer case: A system uses a long stable policy prompt for many requests. Place stable instructions before request-specific data when the selected model’s caching behavior supports that pattern. Exclude private user data from cross-user cache assumptions. Measure cache use and answer quality after the change.
Misconception correction: Cache reuse is conditional on supported models and request details. It is neither automatic for every request nor permission to share private context.

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Cost control begins with attribution. Associate requests with an application, task type, and model route where policy permits. Compare cost per accepted task instead of raw cost per call. A system with retries or agent loops can make several calls for one user request. Cache only eligible stable content, and protect isolation across users. Reduce irrelevant retrieved text and repeated history before lowering model capability. Review cache behavior after prompt edits because a small prefix change can affect reuse.

invariant: Caching can reduce repeated eligible processing, while each request still requires correct isolation and full cost accounting.

steps: Choose a supported model and record current prompt token usage and cache metrics.
Move the stable instruction block before the variable user content without changing text.
Repeat the same request sequence and record cache signals, latency, and answer quality.
Compare with a sequence that changes the stable prefix.
experiment.prediction: A stable repeated prefix can improve reuse when the model and API support the cache path.
experiment.interpretation: Retain the ordering only when measured reuse improves and request isolation remains correct.

transferQuestion: Predict why a longer prompt can raise cost even when the output stays short.
transferAnswer: The request still processes more input context. Reuse stable content where supported and remove irrelevant context.

title: Throughput and latency
idea: Throughput measures completed work over time, while latency measures time for one request.

sections.title: The smallest unit
paragraphs: Users experience latency from the full request path. It can include authentication, retrieval, model queueing, generation, tool calls, and network transfer. Throughput depends on service capacity, request shape, concurrency, and downstream limits.

sections.title: How the mechanism works
paragraphs: Streaming can show early output sooner without reducing total generation time. A smaller prompt can reduce input work. Parallel retrieval can reduce sequential wait when dependencies allow it. More concurrency can increase throughput until a shared limit or bottleneck appears. Measure under realistic request sizes and traffic patterns.

sections.title: Where it fits
paragraphs: Use percentiles to understand slow requests, not only averages. Separate time spent in retrieval, model calls, tools, and application code. Apply timeouts that fit the user task. Avoid unbounded concurrency or retries because they can worsen overload.

sections.title: Failure and control
paragraphs: Load tests should include normal and peak patterns, cold paths, large requests, and service errors. Confirm current quotas and capacity plans in the relevant account and Region.

sections.title: Causal worked trace
paragraphs: Causal trace: A request enters the application, passes retrieval, calls a model, and may call tools. Each stage adds time. Streaming can expose the first model output before generation ends. Concurrency increases active work. When a downstream quota or capacity limit is reached, requests queue or fail. More clients can then increase tail latency instead of throughput.

sections.title: Failure diagnosis
paragraphs: Failure diagnosis: Break latency into application, retrieval, model, tool, and network spans. Compare percentiles and error rates under realistic load. If only high concurrency degrades, inspect queues and quotas. If time to first token improves but total time does not, streaming changed perceived latency rather than total work.

sections.title: Transfer case and misconception
paragraphs: Transfer case: A help desk sees long waits during peak traffic. Measure the full path at normal and peak request rates. Test a smaller prompt and bounded concurrency separately. Confirm current account quotas and deployment capacity before choosing a scaling strategy.
Misconception correction: More parallel requests do not always increase completed work per second. Shared limits can create queueing, throttling, and retry amplification.

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Latency budgets should reflect user needs and dependency behavior. Measure time to first output separately from time to final completion. A streaming design can improve the first measure while total work remains unchanged. Load tests should preserve realistic prompt sizes and retrieval patterns. Include throttling and timeout behavior. Scale one bottleneck at a time. If model time dominates, application parallelism may not help. If retrieval dominates, changing model capacity may have little effect.
Keep load-test results with the tested model route and request profile. A result from a different prompt size or Region may not predict production behavior.
Include a quota test and a recovery test after the load test.

invariant: Throughput improves only while added concurrency stays within the capacity of every required dependency.

steps: Set a representative request mix and fixed request rate.
Change the application concurrency limit from baseline L to a higher bounded value L2.
Measure completion rate, latency percentiles, throttling, and errors.
Repeat at a lower limit to identify the saturation point.
experiment.prediction: Completion rate may rise before saturation, then level off or fall as queues and throttling increase.
experiment.interpretation: Choose a concurrency limit from measured completion rate and latency, with headroom for dependency limits.

transferQuestion: Predict why higher concurrency may worsen both latency and error rates.
transferAnswer: A downstream service can saturate. Requests queue or fail, so control concurrency and observe each dependency.

title: Observability
idea: Observability links request traces, service metrics, and logs to explain system behavior.

sections.title: The smallest unit
paragraphs: Metrics show rates and distributions. Logs record selected events. Traces connect stages in one request. Together they help locate delay, failure, and quality changes. Model text can be sensitive, so observability must include data minimization.

sections.title: How the mechanism works
paragraphs: Record a request identifier, model or route, prompt version, retrieval outcome, tool names, latency, usage, and error class where policy allows. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging can send invocation data to configured CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3 destinations. Review what content enters those destinations and who can access it.

sections.title: Where it fits
paragraphs: A trace should distinguish retrieval failure from generation failure. It should also show retries and partial stream outcomes. Avoid treating model output alone as a diagnostic record. Keep retention and access aligned with the data classification.

sections.title: Failure and control
paragraphs: Use dashboards for service health and sampled review for answer quality. Alert on actionable conditions such as elevated error rate, latency, or empty retrieval. Do not alert on a metric without an owner and response path.

sections.title: Causal worked trace
paragraphs: Causal trace: The application creates a trace identifier and sends a request. The gateway records route and policy result. Retrieval records safe source identifiers and timing. The model call records route, usage, and outcome. The response path records completion or error. These linked events let an operator locate a failure without storing every sensitive prompt or answer.

sections.title: Failure diagnosis
paragraphs: Failure diagnosis: Check trace continuity across application, gateway, retrieval, model, and tool spans. A missing span indicates instrumentation or propagation gaps. A latency spike points to the slow stage. A quality issue needs evaluation evidence and prompt or retrieval versions. Logs without versions cannot explain behavior changes reliably.

sections.title: Transfer case and misconception
paragraphs: Transfer case: A user reports a stale answer. Use the request identifier to inspect the route, prompt version, retrieval sources, sync age, and model outcome. Limit access to sensitive logs. Compare the retrieved source version with the authoritative object before changing model settings.
Misconception correction: More logging is not automatically better observability. Unneeded prompt capture can raise privacy risk without locating the failure boundary.

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Telemetry should answer specific operational questions. Decide which fields identify a route, version, stage, error, and outcome. Avoid high-cardinality labels that make metrics hard to use. Protect trace access because even metadata can reveal sensitive activity. Set retention based on incident and audit needs. Sample routine requests when full traces are costly, while preserving error traces when policy allows. Ensure operators can find the trace from a user report without exposing the report to every support role.
CloudTrail can support account activity review, while invocation logs support request diagnosis. Select each source for its operational purpose and retention policy.

invariant: A request must have enough safe, linked telemetry to locate its failing stage and configuration.

steps: Choose one synthetic request and enable a trace identifier across application stages.
Add a retrieval timing and source identifier event without full passage text.
Run the request with an induced retrieval delay in a test environment.
Inspect whether the trace identifies retrieval as the delayed stage.
experiment.prediction: Linked stage timing should locate the delay while avoiding full sensitive content in logs.
experiment.interpretation: Keep telemetry fields that answer an operational question. Add content capture only under approved need and controls.

transferQuestion: Predict what diagnostic gap remains if logs record only the final answer.
transferAnswer: The team cannot see which evidence, prompt, model route, or tool result shaped the answer. Record safe request metadata across stages.

title: Evaluation
idea: Evaluation tests whether a system meets defined quality and safety requirements.

sections.title: The smallest unit
paragraphs: A model output can sound plausible and still be wrong. Evaluation starts with explicit criteria and representative examples. A dataset should cover normal requests, edge cases, and known failure risks. Human review may be needed for subjective judgments.

sections.title: How the mechanism works
paragraphs: For RAG, separate retrieval measures from answer measures. Retrieval metrics can assess whether relevant evidence appears among results. Answer checks can assess correctness, relevance, completeness, and grounding. Safety evaluation can test configured policy boundaries. Use the same versioned test set to compare changes.

sections.title: Where it fits
paragraphs: Automated metrics are proxies. They can disagree with expert judgment or reward superficial patterns. Calibrate them against reviewed examples. Record model, prompt, data, and configuration versions with the result. Do not claim quality from a small or unrepresentative sample.

sections.title: Failure and control
paragraphs: Run evaluation before and after changes to model, prompt, chunking, retrieval, or guardrails. Investigate regressions by category. A higher average score can hide a severe failure on a critical use case.

sections.title: Causal worked trace
paragraphs: Causal trace: An evaluation dataset pairs questions with expected evidence or outcomes. A retrieval-only run returns candidate passages. Metrics assess relevance and coverage. A retrieve-and-generate run also evaluates the answer, including correctness, completeness, faithfulness, or citation behavior. If retrieval coverage is poor, answer changes alone can hide the upstream defect.

sections.title: Failure diagnosis
paragraphs: Failure diagnosis: Separate retrieval metrics from generated answer metrics. Inspect examples where context relevance is high but coverage is low. Inspect faithfulness failures when evidence is present. Confirm evaluator limits and human-reviewed examples. An aggregate score can hide critical failure categories or an unrepresentative dataset.

sections.title: Transfer case and misconception
paragraphs: Transfer case: A team changes chunking. Run retrieval-only evaluation first to compare whether expected source passages appear. Then run retrieve-and-generate evaluation to assess answer impact. Keep dataset, model, and prompt fixed for the comparison, then inspect examples behind metric changes.
Misconception correction: A single evaluation score does not prove a system is reliable. Metrics are measures with scope, assumptions, and blind spots.

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Evaluation sets need stable versions and clear expected evidence. Include cases that expose known risks, such as stale sources, missing context, ambiguous questions, and policy exceptions. Keep a holdout set for decisions when repeated tuning may overfit a development set. Record evaluator model and configuration. Review samples where automated metrics disagree with human judgment. A metric can track a trend, but an owner must decide whether the change matters for the intended user and risk.
Do not tune against the final holdout set. Preserve that set for a later check after the chosen configuration is stable.
Document the reason for each acceptance threshold and the owner who approved it.

invariant: A quality claim must match the evaluated task, data, configuration, metric, and known limits.

steps: Select a fixed dataset with questions and expected supporting passages.
Change the retrieval result count from baseline K to K2.
Run retrieve-only evaluation and record context relevance and coverage.
Run retrieve-and-generate evaluation on the same cases and inspect faithfulness and citations.
experiment.prediction: A higher result count may improve coverage while lowering relevance or increasing context noise.
experiment.interpretation: Choose K from both retrieval and answer measures. Review individual failures before accepting an aggregate improvement.

transferQuestion: Predict why answer accuracy alone does not diagnose a RAG failure.
transferAnswer: The answer can be wrong because retrieval missed the evidence or because generation misused it. Measure both stages.

title: Troubleshooting
idea: Troubleshooting locates the first failed boundary and tests a targeted cause.

sections.title: The smallest unit
paragraphs: A model application crosses boundaries: client, identity, API, model access, retrieval, network, and output parsing. Start with the error type and request identifier. Compare expected and actual request shape. Confirm the caller, Region, model route, and permissions.

sections.title: How the mechanism works
paragraphs: Access denied points toward identity or resource policy. Throttling points toward quota or burst behavior. Validation errors point toward request shape or unsupported settings. A timeout can mean the client ended before the service completed. A service error can be transient, but repeated retries can hide the real cause.

sections.title: Where it fits
paragraphs: Reproduce with the smallest request that preserves the fault. Change one variable at a time. Check current service documentation for the named error and model support. Keep secrets out of diagnostic output. Confirm whether any side effect completed before retrying a timed-out tool action.

sections.title: Failure and control
paragraphs: After a fix, test the original path and the failure case. Record the root cause and prevention control. A workaround that increases retries may reduce symptoms while raising cost and load.

sections.title: Causal worked trace
paragraphs: Causal trace: A client sends a request with a model identifier and body. The service returns an error class and request information. The application classifies the error as access, validation, throttling, timeout, or service failure. It checks configuration or applies a bounded retry only where appropriate. If the same invalid parameter is retried, the same validation failure repeats without progress.

sections.title: Failure diagnosis
paragraphs: Failure diagnosis: Read the error class before changing code. Access denial requires identity or policy review. Validation requires payload or model setting correction. Throttling requires quota and rate handling. Timeouts require checking completion state. Service errors may be transient. Preserve request identifiers while removing secrets from diagnostics.

sections.title: Transfer case and misconception
paragraphs: Transfer case: An application sees throttling during a burst. Inspect attempt rates and account quota. Apply bounded backoff with jitter and cap concurrent work. Re-test under expected traffic. If errors persist at normal demand, review quota or capacity rather than increasing retries.
Misconception correction: Retrying every error does not improve resilience. It can repeat permanent failures and amplify load during an outage.

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Use a decision tree that starts with error class and request state. Confirm whether the service received the request and whether an external action may have completed. Capture request identifiers and relevant configuration while redacting credentials and personal data. Check service status and quotas only when the error points there. Change one cause at a time. Document the verified root cause and prevention step. This avoids turning a temporary workaround into permanent retry behavior.
Separate client-side timeouts from service errors. A client timeout does not prove that the service stopped processing the request.

invariant: The recovery action must match the diagnosed error class and the operation’s repeat safety.

steps: Use a test request that returns a known throttling response.
Set a bounded retry policy with backoff for throttling only.
Repeat with a validation error and confirm that it receives no retry.
Record attempts, final result, and elapsed time.
experiment.prediction: The throttled request can recover when service capacity returns. The invalid request stops after its first validation failure.
experiment.interpretation: Keep error-specific retry rules and bounded attempts. Correct permanent request or permission defects directly.

transferQuestion: Predict the right first action for a validation error caused by an unsupported parameter.
transferAnswer: Remove or correct the parameter according to the model API. Retrying the same request will repeat the same failure.

title: CI/CD for AI applications
idea: CI/CD applies repeatable checks and controlled release steps to AI system changes.

sections.title: The smallest unit
paragraphs: An AI application has code plus behavior configuration. Prompts, evaluation data, retrieval settings, guardrails, model routes, and infrastructure can all change output. A release process should identify each changed component and its owner.

sections.title: How the mechanism works
paragraphs: Use source control for prompts and infrastructure where possible. Run schema checks, security checks, and evaluation before release. Deploy to a test environment with representative data controls. Promote a version only when it meets the release criteria. Keep the prior version available for rollback.

sections.title: Where it fits
paragraphs: Model behavior can change when a provider updates a model or when the application changes its context. Pin supported versions where the service offers that control. Record the exact route and settings used in evaluation. Use staged rollout for changes with broad user impact.

sections.title: Failure and control
paragraphs: A deployment pipeline cannot prove every answer is safe. It can make known checks repeatable and expose regressions before broad release. Pair automated checks with human review for high-impact cases.

sections.title: Causal worked trace
paragraphs: Causal trace: A developer changes a prompt, model route, or retrieval setting. Source control records the change. CI validates schemas and runs the evaluation set. A release gate compares results with acceptance criteria. Deployment promotes the approved version. A rollback restores the prior version if production signals regress. If prompts are outside source control, code checks can pass while behavior changes unnoticed.

sections.title: Failure diagnosis
paragraphs: Failure diagnosis: Identify which artifact changed, then compare its evaluated version with the deployed version. Check data and model route alongside code. If CI passed but production fails, compare environment, identity, source freshness, and traffic pattern. An evaluation pass covers only its cases and must not be treated as universal proof.

sections.title: Transfer case and misconception
paragraphs: Transfer case: A team updates a prompt and tool schema in one release. Version both artifacts. Run schema checks, security checks, and task evaluation. Deploy to a test environment with safe representative data. Promote only after approval, and retain the prior prompt and configuration for rollback.
Misconception correction: CI/CD can repeat known checks and control release steps. It cannot prove every possible model response is correct or safe.

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Treat prompts, evaluation cases, retrieval configuration, guardrail settings, and infrastructure as release artifacts. A pipeline can lint schemas, run tests, compare evaluation results, and require approvals. Use environment-specific identities and data. Keep secrets in managed secret stores, not source control. Stage broad changes when practical and monitor post-release indicators. Define rollback triggers before release. A rollback must restore compatible model, prompt, index, and tool versions, not only application code.
For RAG releases, record the index or sync state used by evaluation. A prompt check against stale test data may not predict production answers.

invariant: Every behavior-affecting artifact must be versioned, evaluated, and traceable to the deployed release.

steps: Select a prompt and evaluation baseline under version control.
Change one prompt instruction and commit the new version.
Run the release pipeline and compare evaluation output with the baseline.
Attempt promotion with the old evaluation record, then with a record for the new version.
experiment.prediction: A version-aware gate should reject a candidate whose evaluation record does not match the changed prompt.
experiment.interpretation: Bind evaluation evidence to exact artifact versions. Keep promotion and rollback tied to those versions.

transferQuestion: Predict why a code-only pipeline misses a prompt regression.
transferAnswer: Prompt text can change behavior without changing application code. Version and evaluate prompts as release inputs.
